newsitem.title: CANADA: CP sells some U.S. track for US$250 mln.
newsitem.headline: CP sells some U.S. track for US$250 mln.

text.p: Canadian Pacific Ltd unit Canadian Pacific Railway (CPR) said on Friday that it concluded the sale of 1,839 km (1,143 miles) of its lines and associated assets in the midwestern United States to I&M Rail Link (IMRL) for US$250-million.
The new railway, which is based in Davenport, Iowa, will begin operations on April 5. The company is majority-owned by Dennis Washington, of Missoula, Mont., CPR said.

"The deal ensures continued, competitive rail service and employment in the region, and it introduces a strong, new player, I&M Rail Link, to the transportation marketplace," Robert Ritchie, president and chief executive officer of CPR, said in a statement.
"We have full confidence in this new venture and in the important markets the IMRL network serves." he said.

The agreement calls for the sale of a 826-km (513-mile) rail line between Kansas City and Pingree Grove, Ill., just outside Chicago, including a branchline into Wisconsin, and 1,013 km (630 miles) of rail lines in northern Iowa and southern Minnesota. It includes associated rail properties and facilities in Illinois, Iowa, Missouri, Minnesota and Wisconsin.
In a separate transaction, CPR also has sold 24 locomotives and nearly 1,000 railcars to the new company.

A majority of the IMRL employees on the affected lines were employees of CPR. The IMRL employees are represented by the Brotherhood of Locomotive Engineers and the Brotherhood of Maintenance of Way Employees. CPR employees electing not to accept employment with IMRL are covered by provisions of their current labor contracts.
"We are looking forward to meeting with all our new customers, to assist them with their transportation plans," said Bill Brodsky, president of IMRL.

As previously announced, CPR has acquired a one-third equity interest in IMRL, which has been put into an independent voting trust, pending its request for a declaratory order from the Surface Transportation Board allowing it to directly control its interest. The Board said it would evaluate the implications of CPR's minority interest as a separate matter.

The sale provides CPR with a significant injection of capital and, at the same time, puts the railway on course in its plan to restructure its North American network, Mr. Ritchie said. ((Reuters Montreal bureau 514-985-2434))
